stem: A Tier 1 analyst receives a SIEM alert: 14 failed logins followed by a successful login to a finance server. Following a standard SOC workflow, what should the analyst do NEXT?

options.text: Reimage the finance server immediately to remove any attacker access.
options.why: Containment before triage skips a step: you don't yet know whether this is a real incident, and reimaging destroys evidence.

options.text: Triage the alert: check the source, account, timing and context to decide whether it is a true positive.
options.why: Correct. Triage (real or noise?) comes right after an alert fires and decides whether to investigate further or close.

options.text: Close the alert as noise because the login eventually succeeded.
options.why: A success after many failures is the classic sign of a guessed password. It is a reason to look closer, not to close.

options.text: Escalate straight to the SOC manager before looking at it.
options.why: The SOC manager owns oversight and escalation policy, not first-look triage. Escalating without triage wastes senior time.

explanation: The SOC workflow runs: alert → triage → investigation → escalation if needed → containment/remediation → documentation. Triage comes first so analysts spend time on real threats.

stem: A SOC is redefining its tiers. Which TWO responsibilities belong at Tier 3 rather than Tier 1? (Choose two.)

options.text: Proactive threat hunting for activity that hasn't triggered alerts
options.why: Correct. Hunting assumes compromise and searches beyond existing alerts, which is Tier 3 work.

options.text: Watching the alert queue and doing initial triage
options.why: This is the core Tier 1 job.

options.text: Advanced analysis such as reverse-engineering a malware sample
options.why: Correct. Deep technical analysis sits at Tier 3.

options.text: Owning SOC metrics and the escalation policy
options.why: This is the SOC manager's role (oversight, metrics, escalation ownership), not an analyst tier.

explanation: Tier 1 triages, Tier 2 investigates in depth, Tier 3 hunts threats and does advanced analysis, and the SOC manager owns oversight and metrics.

stem: A SOC lead reviews this weekly rule report. Which action would BEST reduce analyst workload without losing the rule's detection value?
artifact:
SOC weekly rule report (week 40)
Rule: VPN-ImpossibleTravel-01
Alerts fired:            214
Closed false positive:   133 (62%)
  top FP reason: user egress via corporate VPN concentrator 198.51.100.10
True positive:           4
Median triage time:      41 min

options.text: Tune the rule to exclude the known corporate VPN egress address, then keep tracking its true/false-positive rate.
options.why: Correct. The false positives share one known, benign cause. Tuning that out keeps the rule's real detections and frees triage time.

options.text: Disable the rule, since 62% of its alerts are false positives.
options.why: It still caught 4 true positives. Turning it off removes detection completely.

options.text: Hire more Tier 1 analysts to absorb the alert volume.
options.why: This treats the symptom. The noise remains and triage still costs 41 minutes per alert.

options.text: Review this rule's alerts in a weekly batch instead of in real time.
options.why: This gives up continuous monitoring, so a real impossible-travel login could go unanswered for days.

explanation: Process improvement (1.5) targets the root cause of noise. One documented false-positive source makes a precise tuning candidate, and measuring precision afterwards confirms the change worked.

stem: A company moves its HR application from its own data centre to an IaaS provider. Under the shared responsibility model, which task does the company STILL own?

options.text: Physical security of the provider's data centre
options.why: The provider owns physical facilities in every cloud model.

options.text: Patching the hypervisors that host the virtual machines
options.why: The IaaS provider manages the virtualisation layer.

options.text: Configuring IAM permissions and protecting the data in its workloads
options.why: Correct. Identities, configurations, workloads and data stay with the customer.

options.text: Replacing failed storage hardware
options.why: Hardware is the provider's responsibility.

explanation: Cloud shifts physical infrastructure to the provider, but the customer always keeps its data, identities (IAM) and the security of its workload configurations.

stem: In a software-defined network, a central controller calculates paths and pushes flow rules to the switches. Which SDN plane is the controller operating in?

options.text: Data plane
options.why: The data plane forwards packets according to the rules it has received. It doesn't decide them.

options.text: Control plane
options.why: Correct. The control plane decides how traffic should flow and programs the data plane.

options.text: Management plane
options.why: The management plane handles admin access, configuration and monitoring of the devices.

options.text: Data link layer (Layer 2)
options.why: This is an OSI layer, not one of the three SDN planes.

explanation: SDN separates the control plane (decisions, centralised in the controller) from the data plane (forwarding). The management plane covers administration. Centralised control means faster, consistent policy changes.

stem: An analyst correlates these events from a hybrid environment. What should the analyst do FIRST?
artifact:
[onprem-dc01] 2026-10-08T02:14:07Z EventID=4624 LogonType=10 User=CORP\j.tan Src=203.0.113.50
[cloudtrail]  2026-10-08T02:16:42Z eventName=ConsoleLogin user=j.tan sourceIPAddress=203.0.113.50 MFAUsed=No
[cloudtrail]  2026-10-08T02:18:03Z eventName=CreateAccessKey user=j.tan sourceIPAddress=203.0.113.50

options.text: Treat j.tan's identity as compromised across both environments: disable the new access key and the account per the playbook, then investigate.
options.why: Correct. The same external IP reached on-prem RDP and the cloud console without MFA, then created a persistent credential. The identity is the attack path, so contain it.

options.text: Ignore the cloud events; the provider is responsible for securing console logins.
options.why: Under shared responsibility, identities and IAM belong to the customer.

options.text: Block 203.0.113.50 at the on-prem perimeter firewall and close the case.
options.why: The cloud console is reached over the internet, not through your perimeter. The new access key also works from any IP.

options.text: Open a ticket asking the cloud provider to investigate the login.
options.why: The provider won't investigate your IAM users' activity for you. This delays containment.

explanation: In cloud/hybrid environments IAM is the perimeter. One external IP using one identity on-prem and in the cloud, with no MFA and a new access key created (persistence), calls for containing the identity first.

stem: A storage bucket was exposed publicly by a Terraform template that went through code review unnoticed. Which control would BEST stop the same mistake reaching production again?

options.text: Scan IaC templates in the CI pipeline (e.g. with Checkov) and fail the build on public-exposure findings
options.why: Correct. It catches the misconfiguration before deployment by treating infrastructure templates as code that needs security review.

options.text: Rely on GuardDuty to alert after resources are deployed
options.why: This is a detective control that fires after exposure, and it isn't designed as a misconfiguration scanner.

options.text: Have an engineer check the cloud console by hand after every deployment
options.why: This happens after deployment and doesn't scale with frequent deploys.

options.text: Move the workload back on-premises
options.why: This avoids the risk out of proportion to it, and the root cause (unchecked templates) isn't addressed.

explanation: IaC misconfigurations are a top cloud attack vector. Pre-deployment scanning (Checkov, Prisma Cloud) is the preventive control. Runtime detection is a backstop, not a replacement.

stem: An analyst is investigating suspicious activity in an AWS account. Which TWO log sources are generated natively by AWS and most relevant? (Choose two.)

options.text: AWS CloudTrail
options.why: Correct. It records API and console activity: who did what, from where.

options.text: VPC Flow Logs
options.why: Correct. They capture network flow metadata for traffic in the VPC.

options.text: Microsoft Sentinel
options.why: This is Azure's cloud SIEM. It can ingest AWS logs, but it isn't an AWS log source.

options.text: Azure Activity Log
options.why: This records Azure control-plane events, not AWS.

explanation: Know the platform-native sources. AWS: CloudTrail (API activity), VPC Flow Logs (network) and GuardDuty (threat detection). Azure: Sentinel (SIEM) and Defender for Cloud.

stem: After a cloud incident, the team wants to map the attacker's behaviour (abusing valid cloud accounts, discovering storage, exfiltrating to an external bucket) to a standard adversary framework. Which reference fits BEST?

options.text: MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix
options.why: Correct. It catalogues adversary tactics and techniques specific to cloud platforms.

options.text: OWASP API Security Top 10
options.why: This lists API vulnerability classes, not adversary behaviour across an intrusion.

options.text: CVSS
options.why: CVSS scores the severity of individual vulnerabilities. It doesn't map attacker behaviour.

options.text: NIST CSF
options.why: This is a program-level framework (Identify, Protect…) and doesn't catalogue techniques.

explanation: The ATT&CK Cloud Matrix is the tactical reference for mapping cloud incidents to adversary tactics and techniques.

stem: A security lead says perimeter-focused monitoring won't protect a new app built from microservices, serverless functions and short-lived containers. Which characteristic BEST explains why?

options.text: The attack surface is distributed across many small, ephemeral components and APIs
options.why: Correct. Many fast-changing parts talk over APIs, so there is no single chokepoint to watch.

options.text: Cloud providers do not allow customers to collect logs from serverless functions
options.why: False. Providers offer native logging for these services.

options.text: Serverless functions run on the customer's own hardware
options.why: False. Serverless runs on provider-managed infrastructure.

options.text: The shared responsibility model no longer applies to cloud-native apps
options.why: False. Customers still secure their workloads and configurations.

explanation: The core cloud-native challenge is the distributed, ephemeral attack surface. Monitoring has to follow the workloads and APIs, using cloud-native tools.

stem: A vendor advisory describes a flaw that lets code in a guest VM execute on the underlying host. What is this attack, and what is the primary mitigation?

options.text: VM escape; keep the hypervisor patched
options.why: Correct. Breaking out of the guest's isolation is VM escape, the most severe virtualisation-specific attack. Patching the hypervisor closes it.

options.text: VM sprawl; inventory VMs against the asset list
options.why: Sprawl is about forgotten, unmanaged VMs, not breaking isolation.

options.text: VM escape; take snapshots of every guest
options.why: Snapshots don't prevent escape, and they can hold sensitive data themselves.

options.text: Container escape; stop running containers as root
options.why: Wrong technology. This describes a hypervisor and guest VM, not containers.

explanation: VM escape bypasses isolation and can expose every VM on the host, which makes hypervisor patching critical.

stem: This reconciliation report was produced during a quarterly review. What issue does it show, and what is the BEST next step?
artifact:
VM inventory reconciliation (cluster: prod-esx-02)
VM name        Power  Guest OS             Last patched  In asset list?
fin-app-01     On     Windows Server 2022  2026-09-28    yes
test-sql-old   On     Windows Server 2016  2023-11-02    no
jdoe-poc-web   On     Ubuntu 20.04         2024-02-19    no
hr-portal-02   On     Ubuntu 24.04         2026-10-01    yes

options.text: VM sprawl. Find owners for the unlisted VMs, then patch and register them, or decommission them.
options.why: Correct. Running VMs missing from the asset list, unpatched for years, are textbook sprawl and easy targets.

options.text: VM escape. Patch the hypervisor cluster immediately.
options.why: Nothing here shows a guest breaking isolation.

options.text: Nothing to fix. Test VMs are short-lived and don't need patching.
options.why: These have been running for years. Unpatched and powered on, they are attackable.

options.text: Delete every unlisted VM immediately without contacting anyone.
options.why: Deleting without checking ownership could destroy something the business needs. Gaps should be handled deliberately.

explanation: Inventory VMs regularly and cross-reference them with the active asset list. Unknown VMs need an owner, then patching or decommissioning.

stem: An analyst suspects lateral movement between two VMs on the same host, but the perimeter firewall logs show nothing. What would BEST give visibility of this traffic?

options.text: Micro-segmentation and monitoring at the virtual network layer (e.g. a distributed firewall such as VMware NSX)
options.why: Correct. East-west traffic between VMs never crosses the perimeter, so visibility has to come from inside the virtual network.

options.text: More rules on the perimeter firewall
options.why: The traffic never reaches the perimeter, so new rules there will never see it.

options.text: Monitoring snapshot creation events
options.why: Useful in investigations, but it doesn't show network traffic between VMs.

options.text: Moving the VMs to a Type 2 hypervisor
options.why: Type 2 hypervisors are for labs and desktops. This adds no visibility.

explanation: East-west traffic between VMs stays inside the host or virtual switch. Micro-segmentation tools give the virtual network layer both visibility and control.

stem: During a test, an attacker breaks out of a compromised container. Why can the impact be greater than a single compromised application?

options.text: Containers share the host OS kernel, so an escape can reach the host and every other container on it
options.why: Correct. The shared kernel is the core container risk.

options.text: Each container runs its own full OS kernel, so the attacker gets a second kernel
options.why: Backwards. Containers don't have their own kernels; VMs do.

options.text: Containers cannot be monitored at runtime
options.why: False. Tools such as Falco monitor container runtime behaviour.

options.text: Container images are always pulled from public registries
options.why: False, and it doesn't explain the blast radius of an escape.

explanation: Containers are lightweight because they share the host kernel. That same sharing means a container escape can compromise the host and its neighbours.

stem: This Falco alert fires for a production pod. What is the BEST interpretation and response?
artifact:
10:42:17.311 Notice A shell was spawned in a container with an attached terminal
  rule=Terminal shell in container  user=root  shell=bash  parent=runc
  k8s.ns=prod  k8s.pod=payments-api-7d9f6c-x2kqp
  image=registry.example.com/payments-api:2.3.1

options.text: Someone opened an interactive root shell in a production container. Check the Kubernetes audit log for who ran the exec, and contain the pod while investigating.
options.why: Correct. Interactive shells in production containers are rare and risky. The audit log shows the API-level who and how.

options.text: Benign. Falco raises this alert every time a container starts.
options.why: False. This rule fires when a shell with a terminal is spawned, not at container start.

options.text: Rescan the image with Trivy and close the alert if no vulnerabilities are found
options.why: An image scan says nothing about who is running commands in a live container. This skips the investigation.

options.text: Disable the rule to cut noise from production
options.why: This removes visibility of one of the most important runtime signals.

explanation: Falco gives runtime visibility inside containers, and the Kubernetes audit log gives API-level visibility (e.g. who ran kubectl exec). Together they are the analyst's main tools.

stem: A security review of the company's Kubernetes clusters is being scoped. Which TWO findings are common Kubernetes-specific attack vectors? (Choose two.)

options.text: Overly permissive RBAC role bindings
options.why: Correct. RBAC misconfiguration is a top Kubernetes attack vector.

options.text: Secrets stored in plaintext in manifests or environment variables
options.why: Correct. Plaintext secrets are easy to steal once an attacker has any foothold.

options.text: VM sprawl on the hypervisor cluster
options.why: A virtualisation issue, not a Kubernetes-specific one.

options.text: Type 2 hypervisors used in production
options.why: This is about hypervisor choice, not Kubernetes.

explanation: Top Kubernetes attack vectors: RBAC misconfigurations, exposed API servers and plaintext secrets.

stem: Developers want to deploy a popular image straight from a public registry to production. Which control should be applied FIRST?

options.text: Scan the image for vulnerabilities (e.g. with Trivy) and promote it through a trusted internal registry
options.why: Correct. Scanning before deployment is the core image-security control.

options.text: Run the container as root to avoid permission errors
options.why: The opposite of least privilege. Containers shouldn't run as root in production.

options.text: Deploy it and rely on Falco to catch problems
options.why: Falco is runtime detection. A known-vulnerable image should be stopped before it runs.

options.text: Trust it because of its high download count
options.why: Popularity isn't a security control. Public images can be malicious or outdated.

explanation: Never pull public images blindly. Scan them before deployment (Trivy, Prisma Cloud) and apply least privilege at the container level.

stem: An analyst reviews these API gateway logs. What BEST describes the activity?
artifact:
gw-access.log (api.example.com)
2026-10-09T14:03:11Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10231 200 1.2KB
2026-10-09T14:03:11Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10232 200 1.1KB
2026-10-09T14:03:12Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10233 200 1.3KB
2026-10-09T14:03:12Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10234 200 1.2KB
... 1,812 similar requests in 6 minutes, all HTTP 200

options.text: Enumeration exploiting Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA): one customer's token is retrieving other customers' invoices
options.why: Correct. Sequential object IDs, all returning 200 to a single user, mean the API isn't checking that the caller owns each object.

options.text: Credential stuffing against the login endpoint
options.why: The requests are already authenticated and target invoice objects, not the login endpoint.

options.text: A volumetric denial-of-service attack
options.why: About 5 requests per second retrieving data is data theft, not an attempt to exhaust capacity.

options.text: Normal pagination by a client application
options.why: Pagination uses page or offset parameters. Walking object IDs that belong to other customers is not normal behaviour.

explanation: BOLA, top of the OWASP API Security Top 10, lets an authenticated user access objects they don't own by changing IDs. API gateways should alert on sequential enumeration patterns.

stem: The billing-sync service's API key normally calls the API from 192.0.2.15. The gateway now shows the activity below. What should the analyst do FIRST?
artifact:
api-key: key_live_8f3a...c21 (owner: billing-sync service)
2026-10-09T01:12:44Z src=203.0.113.200 GET /api/v1/customers?limit=500 200
2026-10-09T01:12:51Z src=203.0.113.200 GET /api/v1/customers?offset=500&limit=500 200
2026-10-09T01:13:02Z src=203.0.113.200 GET /api/v1/customers?offset=1000&limit=500 200

options.text: Revoke and rotate the key, then find out how it leaked and what data it accessed
options.why: Correct. A key used from an unexpected location while bulk-pulling customer data means stopping the exfiltration is the priority.

options.text: Add rate limiting to the customers endpoint
options.why: This slows the theft but doesn't stop it. The key is still valid.

options.text: Block 192.0.2.15 at the gateway
options.why: That's the legitimate service's address. It breaks billing and doesn't stop the attacker.

options.text: Monitor for another hour to confirm the pattern
options.why: Customer records are leaving right now. Waiting increases the damage.

explanation: API keys and OAuth tokens are the primary API credentials, and key leakage is a major attack vector. Monitor for keys used from unexpected locations. When it happens, revoke first, then scope and find the leak (e.g. a committed secret).

stem: A company exposes dozens of REST APIs to partners. Where is the BEST place to centrally log and control API activity, such as authentication failures and request rates?

options.text: The API gateway
options.why: Correct. It sits in front of the APIs and can authenticate, rate-limit and log every call.

options.text: The perimeter firewall
options.why: It sees encrypted HTTPS sessions, not API-level details like the endpoint, user or object ID.

options.text: EDR on developer laptops
options.why: Endpoint telemetry doesn't capture partner API traffic.

options.text: The hypervisor logs
options.why: These record VM and host events, not API requests.

explanation: API gateways are the main point for monitoring and controlling API activity. Log everything there and watch for auth failures, high request rates and enumeration.

stem: Why do API attacks often get past traditional network security tools?

options.text: REST API calls travel over HTTP(S) and look like ordinary web traffic
options.why: Correct. Without API-aware inspection, an attack request looks the same as a legitimate one.

options.text: APIs use proprietary non-IP protocols that tools can't parse
options.why: False. REST APIs use standard HTTP over TCP/IP.

options.text: APIs are only reachable from inside the corporate network
options.why: False. Many APIs are deliberately internet-facing.

options.text: API traffic cannot be logged
options.why: False. Gateways and applications can log API calls in detail.

explanation: API attacks blend into normal web traffic, which is why API-aware monitoring at the gateway matters.

stem: Contractors will use their personal phones for corporate email and files. Legal says the company must not control or wipe the whole device. Which approach fits BEST?

options.text: Mobile Application Management (MAM) for the corporate apps and data
options.why: Correct. MAM manages only corporate apps and data, the right fit for BYOD.

options.text: Mobile Device Management (MDM) enrolment of each phone
options.why: MDM manages the entire device, which goes beyond what Legal allows here.

options.text: Install EDR on the contractors' phones
options.why: EDR doesn't address separating and controlling corporate data on a personal device.

options.text: Require full-device encryption and do nothing else
options.why: Encryption protects data at rest but doesn't control or remove corporate data in apps.

explanation: MDM manages corporate-owned devices end to end. MAM manages corporate apps and data only, which makes it the BYOD choice.

stem: An analyst reviews this conditional access sign-in log. Which entry should be investigated FIRST?
artifact:
Conditional access sign-ins
Time   User      Device        Compliant  Policy result  Outcome
07:58  a.lim     LT-0412       Yes        Grant (MFA)    Success
08:03  r.osman   LT-0377       No         Block          Failure
08:11  k.wong    unregistered  No         Not applied    Success
08:15  a.lim     LT-0412       Yes        Grant (MFA)    Success

options.text: 08:11, k.wong: success from an unregistered, non-compliant device where no policy was applied
options.why: Correct. An unexpected success is a gap in zero-trust enforcement, a possible bypass or misconfiguration.

options.text: 08:03, r.osman: blocked from a non-compliant device
options.why: The policy worked as intended. Follow up on the device's compliance later; it isn't the urgent item.

options.text: 07:58, a.lim: compliant device, MFA satisfied
options.why: A normal, expected sign-in.

options.text: 08:15, a.lim: second successful sign-in
options.why: Repeated compliant, MFA-backed sign-ins are normal.

explanation: Monitor conditional access logs for compliance failures and, more importantly, unexpected successes. Access that should have been checked but wasn't is the real risk.

stem: Facilities wants to connect smart HVAC sensors and lobby displays to the office network. These devices can't run EDR or be enrolled in management. What is the BEST control?

options.text: Put them on a dedicated, segmented VLAN with restricted access to corporate systems
options.why: Correct. If you can't manage a device, contain it. Segmentation limits what a compromised IoT device can reach.

options.text: Install EDR agents on them anyway
options.why: These devices typically can't run standard security agents.

options.text: Enrol them in MAM
options.why: MAM manages corporate apps on mobile devices. It doesn't apply to IoT sensors.

options.text: Connect them to the main network; they hold no sensitive data
options.why: They can still be a pivot point into systems that do hold sensitive data.

explanation: IoT devices are high risk and usually can't be managed with standard tools. Segment them away from corporate systems.

stem: During an investigation, an analyst must quickly list which company devices accessed a file server last week and whether each was patched and compliant. What is the BEST starting point?

options.text: The Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) console
options.why: Correct. UEM manages the whole device fleet from one console, the starting point for inventory and compliance checks.

options.text: The perimeter firewall logs
options.why: These show connections at the edge, not device inventory or compliance state.

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the internet-facing range
options.why: Wrong scope. It doesn't cover internal devices' compliance.

options.text: Each user's browser history
options.why: Not an authoritative or scalable source for device posture.

explanation: UEM is the modern single console for the full fleet: inventory, compliance and posture during investigations.
